name: PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk

frontmatter.title: DSSA: the parts, the upstream and the premium
frontmatter.summary: DSSA is a Sinar Mas conglomerate whose coal arm is separately listed. The parts are worth Rp206 in twelve months and Rp183 today; the price is 3.4x today's value. The konglo lens keeps only part of the premium, giving Rp441 and a SELL. OJK's restitution work states no amount and changes no input. The parent collects the October interim and should collect the final by June 2027; it has never paid a dividend.
thesis: The parts — the listed coal stake at the covered subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental value, the non-coal segments at audited net book, the unallocated remainder, net of non-controlling interests and less a holding-company discount — are worth Rp206 after twelve months, far below the Rp625 price.
The own-history P/E and P/BV are dropped, not down-weighted: they are struck on the price history OJK found manipulated and sit several times above the parts.

The upstream is real: the parent receives its controlling share of the October interim and is expected to receive the FY2026 final payable by June 2027, carried below certainty because it is a forecast. The parent has never paid a dividend to its own holders, so the discount is a hoarding discount and is charged at the wide end of the house band.

Power is marked at audited segment net assets because no external replacement-cost or regulated-asset estimate is published; the sensitivity to a lower book mark is disclosed, and technology is tested against its positive segment result.

PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the controlling shareholder, is named by OJK as the DSSA-case recipient of the administrative fine over manipulation of trading in DSSA's own shares; the related parties have paid the penalties and the regulator now says a criminal referral may follow, so the konglo lens slows the premium's compression rather than removing it.

blocks.text: **This update records OJK's restitution work and answers the red team; the one model change is the coal stake's mark.** At the BEI Media Gathering in Mandalika on 31 October 2026, reported on 5 November, the regulator said it is calculating the funds that could be returned to investors affected by the DSSA, BREN and CUAN share cases, while stating no amount and no timing and saying it could not yet confirm the mechanism or the sum [S31]. It also described the return of funds to investors as unusual in administrative sanctions, which have more commonly ended in licence revocation or closure [S31]. Because the report names no payer and assigns no liability to DSSA, no amount is inferred or entered: the holding-company discount and the konglo lens flags are unchanged by the news, so the rating stays SELL and the target Rp441, a -29.5% total return at the Rp625 price [S0]. What the event changes is the governance file, and sections five and six carry it: restitution is a new leg of an enforcement track that has already produced the regulator's largest administrative sanctions, and because its size and payer are unstated it is a tail, not a base-case cash cost [S13, S31]. The rest of the record stands. The HSC index deletion is effective: on 2 November 2026 the exchange removed 81 HSC names from the IHSG calculation, including DSSA and its separately listed coal subsidiary GEMS, and redistributed their index weight to the remaining constituents [S30]. On 1 November OJK published its year-to-date list of sanctioned parties and named PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the controlling shareholder, as the DSSA-case recipient of the Rp1.5tn administrative fine, confirming this report's earlier inference that "PT SMT" referred to the controlling shareholder [S26, S10, S14]. The same day the OJK chair opened the route to criminal referral, saying the parties facing criminal sanctions may be announced within the week and that the enforcement track runs from administrative sanctions to criminal prosecution under the una via principle [S27, S26]. The administrative leg had already settled on 30 October, when OJK confirmed the related parties behind the DSSA, BREN and CUAN cases paid the fines in full to the state treasury — IDR2.10tn across the three, the DSSA-related share IDR1.50tn — and stressed that the payers are the parties, not the listed issuers [S21]. The enforcement record itself moves no line in the parts: the konglo lens already carries the finding as a regime flag and it stays, and the criminal and restitution tracks are governance risks in section five, not base-case convictions. The target is not the previous one: the coal stake now enters the SOTP at the subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental value, as the konglo card's 5 November reconciliation requires, and that is the one model change in this revision [S20, VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §4, S9].

**Revision after the red team.** Six changes, all disclosed rather than buried. The coal stake is marked at the subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental, not its post-lens house target, so no sibling regime premium is carried twice; the target moves accordingly and section four shows the derivation [S20, F100]. The bear leg is disclosed as a discount-only value: the 30% weight is set against the conditional asset tail, which is stated separately and would take the weighted fundamental about a tenth lower if capitalised [S20, S9]. The restitution payer question is tested in section five — issuer, controller or brokers — with the controller's cash-call route and the checked absence of a disclosed pledge [S21, S26, S31, F74]. The statement is dated 31 October, not 5 November, throughout [S31]. The gross-margin challenge is rebutted on the segment note: the non-coal parts earn a higher gross margin than the coal subsidiary, so the group-wide ratio does not overstate them [S9, F112-F115]. And the joint-bull path is stated alongside the joint-bear under the same independence convention [S0, S20]. The prior round's changes stand: the non-controlling-interest bridge, the wide-end discount, the power book mark and the GEMS free-float deadline [S9, S28, S20].

Two other records stand. The 26 October PPJB under which BSDE unit Surya Inter Wisesa sells 16.6 ha in the D-Hub SEZ at BSD City to DSSA unit SMCCG is priced at Rp3.1tn, 5.7% of the group's 30 June equity and just below an independent appraisal of Rp3.12tn [S29, S23]; it is an affiliate transaction but a fair-value asset swap for the data-centre build, so it does not move the parts and is disclosed in section six. And an IDR1.00tn buyback runs from 19 October 2026 to 18 January 2027 [S28] — the first holdco capital return since 2023 and a dated discount catalyst, but small against the company's market value, so it supports rather than moves the 40% charged. The next paragraphs restate the view the update carries forward.

**The view carries forward: the parts, not the OJK-tainted multiples, set the value; the house carries SELL and the Rp441 target.** The fundamental rests entirely on the parts: the coal stake at the covered subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental value, the non-coal businesses at audited segment net book, plus the unallocated corporate remainder, net of the non-controlling interests that belong to outside holders and less a holding-company discount. That is Rp206 a share after twelve months, or Rp183 today [S0]. The price is Rp625, or 3.4x today's fundamental value and well above the twelve-month value [S0]. The konglo lens keeps part of that premium because a float of 21.5% sets the marginal price: the controller holds 59.9%, treasury holds 19.7% and the rest is public, so the base regime case closes 45% of the log gap for Rp405, and probability-weighted across the three regime scenarios the target is Rp441, a -29.5% total return [S0]. The rating is SELL.

**Three standing corrections.** First, the own-history P/E and P/BV are dropped, not cut to a token weight: they are struck on the tape the regulator found was planned, structured and price-lifted [S10, S13, S14], and because they sat several times above the parts, even a ten per cent weight supplied about half the old fundamental. Second, the parent has received subsidiary dividends: the cash flow records the outside shareholders' share at USD 105m in FY2025 and USD 237m in FY2024 [S9], and the subsidiary's note records a final dividend of USD 500m for FY2024 to all shareholders [S9]; at the 51.0% stake, the controlling share reaches DSSA and is reinvested. Third, the card's holdco deductions are applied: overhead capitalised at ten times the sourced office line, and a tested parent net-debt position [S9, F62].

**The variant view.** The market is not paying for the coal arm, which sits in a separately listed subsidiary valued at a fraction of the parent, nor for the non-coal parts at audited book. It is paying a 3.4x premium to the whole. The konglo lens explains why that premium can persist — thin float, index deletions and a live sanction — but it does not make the premium value. We mark the subsidiary at its pre-lens fundamental value, below both its own quote and its own post-lens house target (Rp6,094/share against Rp6,661/share and Rp7,150/share), so the parent's parts carry no sibling regime premium; the parent's own konglo lens is the only lens applied, once, after the SOTP [S20, VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §4]. The nearest bull catalyst is not a first upstream from the subsidiary, which already happens, but a first distribution from DSSA to its own shareholders.

DSSA reports in US dollars and describes itself as an energy and infrastructure company [S9]. Revenue comes from four segments — captive steam and electricity, fertilizer and chemicals trading, coal mining and trading, and cable television, internet and technology, plus small renewable and other lines [S9].

Coal dominates: mining and trading revenue was 2,488 USD m against group revenue of 2,791.2 [S9, S0]; the audited segment note puts mining at almost nine-tenths of revenue [S9]. The coal business sits in PT Golden Energy Mines Tbk, listed since 2011, in which DSSA holds 51.0% directly [S9, S3]. The mines operate under coal contracts of work (CCoW), whose royalty and permit terms the group flags as a margin risk [S9]. The minority interest of 444.4 is largely the coal subsidiary's outside owners [S9].

The other pillars are smaller. Technology revenue was 212 USD m last year and 170 USD m in the first half, roughly double the prior period [S9, S6]; fertilizer and chemicals was 90.9 USD m; power has no external revenue because the fee is earned inside the group [S9]. The group says the energy pillar funds the build-out of the others, its stated reason for not paying a dividend [S6, S9].

Ownership is concentrated: PT Sinar Mas Tunggal holds 59.9% of issued shares; the audited register puts public and treasury shares together at 40.1%, of which treasury is 19.7%, leaving a public float in the low twenties [S9]. The lens uses the datapack's 21.5% IDX registry figure [S0]; the konglo registry's source field points at the GEMS interim article, which does not contain it, and that correction stays open with the Director [S25]. Both readings clear the raised fifteen per cent minimum [S19]; the subsidiary's own float is the one that does not, and it is set out in section six. OJK's 1 November enforcement list names PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the controlling shareholder, as the DSSA-case recipient of the fine [S26]; the earlier Kompas and Antara reports abbreviated the name to PT SMT [S10, S14]. Market capitalisation is IDR96,707.6bn with about IDR420.5bn traded a day, so no liquidity discount applies [S0]; the fifty-two week range of 432.0 to 4,640.0 shows the repricing [S0].

A listed parent that owns stakes in separately listed children usually trades at a discount to what
those stakes are worth: minority holders cannot direct the cash, cannot force a distribution, and bear
the cost of whatever the parent builds next. The discount narrows only when something specific and
dated forces value up to the parent.

DSSA is five businesses, and the house card says mark each on its own terms rather than apply a blanket multiple to the group [S9]. The largest is thermal coal. The coal price reaches DSSA through the listed subsidiary's own quote and fundamental value, not through a mine model we build here, so the coal path enters the parts as the market's and the subsidiary's own view rather than a second, independent forecast [S9, S12].

Power is a captive processing fee with a large asset base and no external revenue [S9]. Chemicals is a low-margin distribution book [S9]. Digital infrastructure — broadband, homepasses and a data-centre build — is the fastest-growing revenue line [S6, S9]. Competitively, the group is a follower: the coal producer is mid-curve with a wide calorific range and a domestic, China and India customer mix [S9]; broadband and data centres face far larger incumbents in a scale business with front-loaded capital [S6, S9]; chemicals is a price-taker [S9]. Only the power processing agreement has a semblance of a moat, and it is the part with the largest book and the least external revenue [S9].

Two external influences matter: the market-conduct file against the controlling shareholder — whose administrative fines the related parties have now paid, while the criminal file stays open — which the house framework reads as a manipulation-class flag [S10, S14, S21], and the coal royalty and permit regime, which the group flags as a margin risk [S9] and which reaches our target through the subsidiary's model.

Revenue fell to 2,791.2 last year from 3,017.8, and gross margin compressed to 33.7% from 40.7% [S0]. Net profit to the parent was 230.5, of which minorities took 130.7 [S0, S9], and return on equity was 16.0% [S9].

The data pack's depreciation is a fraction of the real charge because the cash-flow statement uses the direct method and carries no add-back; the segment note discloses consolidated D&A of 78.2 USD m and 83.6 USD m for the last two years, and the model carries that restated charge [S9]. Two splits make older per-share metrics not like-for-like [S0].

The forecast is built from the reported first half and the subsidiary's own covered plan, not from last year's ratios: the other non-operating line (44.2) and the minority split (130.7) are carried at the FY2025A actual, the cost of debt is the FY2025 effective rate, and the coal path is the subsidiary's own FY2026E model [S0, S9, S20]. Revenue growth of 30.0% takes the top line to 3,628.6: the first half, reported in [S6] (which describes the interim as audited; the LK itself is not archived), ran US$1,770.0m, up roughly a third, with coal up nearly thirty per cent and technology up nearly ninety per cent [S6], and the subsidiary's model prices FY2026 at the house coal deck's FY2026E marker, close to a quarter above FY2025A, on its 58Mt plan against the 55.0Mt realised in 2025 [S20, S12, F48, F79]. Gross margin of 40.7% is the subsidiary's own modelled FY2026E margin, which expands with the higher marker instead of holding last year's ratio against it; the group-wide ratio is not a blanket application to the non-coal parts: the segment note's own columns show the non-coal segment result on non-coal revenue (942 USD m less 790 USD m on 2,791 USD m less 2,488 USD m) above the coal column's margin in FY2025A, so applying the subsidiary's ratio to all group revenue understates the non-coal contribution rather than overstating it [S9, F112-F115]. That gives EBITDA of 875.1, an EBITDA margin of 24.1% and net profit to the parent of 373.1 [S20, S0]. **The first-half bridge.** The reported first half carried US$174.4m of parent profit against a full-year forecast of 373.1, which leaves a second half above the first and at the subsidiary's own second-half run-rate rather than the half-on-half collapse an unchanged FY2025A margin would imply [S6, S20]. The parent's interest income is mechanically lower than FY2025A and interest expense higher on the larger opening debt, both sourced from the FY2025 balance sheet [S0, S9]. FY2027E revenue growth is set at -14.0% for a sourced reason — the subsidiary's model and the deck carry the FY2027E coal marker below FY2026E on a flat 58Mt volume — and from FY2028E the top line is held because no source supports a further decline [S20]. The path feeds only the zero-weighted earnings cross-checks and does not reach the target, which is the sum of the parts [S0, S9].

Capex of 607.2 against EBITDA of 875.1 leaves free cash flow to the firm of 214.1, and the same comparison was negative last year at -99.4 [S0]: spending absorbs essentially all the businesses generate, concentrated in the non-coal pillars [S9, S6]. The FCFF bridge is EBITDA, less cash tax and capex, plus a working-capital release: operating working capital falls from 610.8 to 477.8, the dollar level the 30 June 2026 balance sheet already reports after the reported first half, a release of {{fin.FY2026E.delta_nwc|abs|money}} shown here rather than buried in the net figure [S0, S6]. It is not a ratio artefact: the engine's three-year default is replaced by that reported level and held flat thereafter. We hold capex at last year's ratio without a source to change it [S0, S9].

The balance sheet carries cash of 575.5, debt of 1,486.2 and minorities of 444.4, for net debt of 910.6 and net debt to EBITDA of 1.9 [S0]. This is not charged twice: each part is valued after its own liabilities [S9]. The latest reported balance sheet, at 30 June 2026, carries net debt about a fifth above the FY2025A level of 910.6 used in the model, after a first half in which both cash and debt rose; the FY2026E net-debt line of 698.6 is a mechanical forecast roll from the FY2025A opening, roughly a third below that reported June level, so it is a cross-check and not anchored on the half-year balance sheet [S6, S0]. The target is unaffected: the parts are marked on audited segment books and the forecast balance sheet does not reach the lens. The parent's bonds are inside the segment marks — segment liabilities of 2,121 USD m are within two per cent of consolidated liabilities (assets of 4,415 USD m less equity of 2,261 USD m) — so netting them again would double-count [S9]. The guarantees are a contingent claim in section six [S9].

**The half-year minority balance.** The pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet carries a minority balance roughly double the audited FY2025A total of 444 USD m, and parent equity plus that minority reconciles to the reported total equity of 3,050 USD m [S6, S0]. The increase is not bridged in any source reviewed: the half-year release discloses the one-for-twenty-five share split, the MoraRepublic merger and the iFLYTEK joint venture but no minority-interest reconciliation, and the H1 LK itself is not archived [S6]. We do not mix the 30 June minority with the 31 December 2025 segment books — the SOTP's assets are the audited year-end books and the half-year asset uplift is not in the marks — so the deduction stays on the same-date audited split. If the increase is permanent and unmatched by assets outside the marks, the deduction rises and the value falls; section four records it as an open reconciliation rather than netting it silently.

**Earnings quality.** Accruals are negative in two of the last three years and marginally positive in the third: operating cash was 330 USD m, 693 USD m and 1,031 USD m against net profit of 361.2, 542.8 and 865.3 [S0, S9]. Cash covered profit in two of the three years and fell short by a whisker in the third, well inside the threshold. Free cash flow to the firm turns negative — -99.4, -139.4, 307.6 [S0] — a capital-spending story, not an accruals one. Technology assets grew from 1,162 USD m to 2,208 USD m in a year [S9]. The regulatory action is not a listing-status action on the issuer, and the penalties are borne, and now paid, by the related parties rather than the issuer [S10, S14, S21]. One sanctioned member is PT SS, whose director received an underwriter-licence freeze [S14, F57]; no DSSA entity or director is among the sanctioned parties [S14].

Related-party purchases were 0.4% of cost of revenues and the related-party slice of G&A was 0.9%, mainly family property, telecom and insurance entities [S9]. The larger exposure is structural: allocating a data centre or broadband network between listed and unlisted vehicles is the family's choice [S9, S6], and the data-centre build already runs through a related party — KMG bought the package for the group's data-centre project from PT LG Sinarmas Technology Solutions for Rp1.2tn [S9, F67].

**PSAK 16.** The power book does not carry a revaluation surplus today: the plants were sold in 2024, the decrease in the surplus was 160 USD m, the cumulative increment transferred to retained earnings was USD 111m, and the surplus line is nil [S9]. **Structure flags**: two splits, the restructuring that moved the subsidiary stake onto the parent's books, the elimination column of -1,954 USD m, and the treasury block of 1,516 million shares, 19.7% of issued capital [S9]. The disclosure items are optics-class; the regulator's finding that trading in DSSA's shares was planned, structured and price-lifting is manipulation-class, and it sits at the controlling shareholder rather than in the issuer's accounts [S10, S13, S14].

The house card values a holding company on its parts, less holdco net debt and a discount the base rate says persists [S0]. The parts carry 100% of the blend: the own-history P/E and P/BV are dropped because both sat several times above the parts and are struck on the tape OJK found manipulated [S0, S10, S13, S14]. The cost of equity is 12.6% and the weighted average cost of capital 10.7%, built in the table [S0].

**The parts.** Each mark is a listed price or an audited segment book; the bridge reconciles to consolidated equity and then cuts the consolidated total back to the parent's share. The coal stake is at the covered subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental twelve-month value of Rp6,094/share, not its quote of Rp7,150/share and not its post-lens house target of Rp6,661/share, because the konglo card as reconciled on 5 November 2026 requires a covered listed subsidiary to enter the parent's fundamental value at its fundamental value: the earlier "house target" wording would have carried the sibling's regime premium inside the parent's parts and then applied the parent's own lens on top, counting the premium twice. The parent's konglo lens is applied once, after the SOTP [S20, VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §4]. The mark is 51.0% of that value; all three GEMS marks come from GEMS.JK's own covered report and model [S20].

| Part | Mark | | --- | --- | | PT Golden Energy Mines Tbk, 51.0% stake | pre-lens fundamental [S20] | | Steam and electricity | net book, fallback [S9] | | Cable TV, internet and technology | net book, fallback [S9] | | Fertilizer and chemicals | net book [S9] | | Renewable energy | net book [S9] | | Other | net book [S9] | | Intra-group elimination | deduction [S9] | | Unallocated corporate and tax remainder | value [S9] | | Non-controlling interests | deduction [S9] |

Marks are assets less liabilities: 2,659 USD m less 668 USD m, 2,208 USD m less 1,114 USD m, 57.4 USD m less 32.6 USD m, 75.2 USD m less 1.0 USD m, 37.6 USD m less 0.6 USD m, the elimination -1,954 USD m less -197 USD m, and the remainder equity 2,261 USD m less segment net assets [S9].

**Power and technology are marked on their own terms.** Power is a captive processing-fee asset with no external revenue and no disclosed segment result — the FY2024 comparative was -0.2m [S9] — so an earnings multiple cannot be struck. It is marked at its audited segment net assets, 2,659 USD m less 668 USD m, which is a paid-in asset base, not a sourced replacement cost: no regulated-asset-base or third-party replacement-cost estimate is published in the LK or in the press reviewed, so the mark is disclosed as a book proxy with a sensitivity from half to full book. At three-quarters of book the part falls by a quarter of its marked value and at half book by half, before the discount; the power row is the largest non-coal part, so that is the largest mark-level risk in the parts after GEMS [S9, F23, F24, F71]. Technology is tested on its segment result: 142 USD m before group operating expense, about an eighth of its net book of 2,208 USD m less 1,114 USD m, and a mid-single-digit return after the FY2024 comparative operating expense of USD 78.6m [S9]. On the roughly doubled first-half revenue run-rate [S6, F20] that return approaches the cost of equity, so audited net book at par is the most likely mark, not caution; a ten per cent haircut is the bear's mark, and any further re-rate needs a disclosed segment return. The data-centre parcels are carried at their independent appraisal, so no option value above book is invented [S29, F92-F94]. The PSAK 16 objection is answered: the plants were sold, the cumulative increment was transferred to retained earnings, and the surplus line is nil [S9, F49, F76].

**The reconciliation.** The segment books are stated in full, so the parts must be cut back to the parent's share. Consolidated equity is 2,261 USD m [S9], which includes all non-controlling interests: 444 USD m in total, of which the coal subsidiary is 350 USD m [S9]. The non-GEMS minority is therefore the difference between those two and is deducted directly. The GEMS deduction is a separate piece, and it is the point the red team tested. At the minority share, the 350 USD m GEMS NCI implies whole GEMS net assets well above the coal segment column's 1,051 USD m less 502 USD m of net book, so a slice of GEMS book — the difference between GEMS's implied whole net assets and the coal column — sits in the other parts, principally the unallocated remainder. The SOTP replaces the coal column with the parent's 51.0% share of the GEMS mark; the residual GEMS book outside the column would otherwise be counted in full against that mark and is removed with the non-GEMS minority. The two pieces together are the deduction in the table: the non-GEMS minority plus the GEMS book left in the other parts. Deducting only the non-GEMS minority, as a subtraction of total NCI less GEMS NCI from the non-controlling-interest note would do, leaves that GEMS book double-counted and overstates the parts by the size of that slice; the gross parts value is unchanged under the full reconstruction. The 30 June 2026 pack minority is not mixed into a 31 December 2025 book valuation; section three records the date-consistency and the unreconciled half-year increase [S9, F77, F78, F72, F73].

**Why audited book, not the first-half equity.** The SOTP starts from the audited FY2025 segment books, not the higher first-half-2026 consolidated equity [S6]. The segment marks are audited and the half-year uplift sits largely in the coal column, which the GEMS mark already replaces at the subsidiary's own value; reading the increase straight into the parent's equity would count that uplift twice. The choice is disclosed, and it is why the valuation does not rise with the first-half equity.

**The holdco bridge.** The parent's bonds and sukuk are inside segment liabilities — segment liabilities of 2,121 USD m are within two per cent of consolidated liabilities, and the Phase IV issue alone was Rp0.3tn of bonds plus Rp1.2tn of sukuk [S9, F68, F69] — so netting them again would double-count. What is not in the marks is parent overhead: the parent-level office expense of USD 3.9m [S9, F62], capitalised at ten times, is the deduction, a floor because the parent-only share of salaries is not published. The guarantees are a contingent claim in section six [S9, F63-F66].

**The upstream, corrected.** The old report said the parent had never received a dividend; that was wrong. The cash flow records NCI dividends of USD 105m in FY2025 and USD 237m in FY2024 [S9], and the subsidiary's note records final dividends of USD 500m for FY2024 and USD 500m for FY2023 to all holders [S9]. At 51.0% the parent receives the controlling share; it covers the capitalised office cost about six and a half times on FY2024 and almost three times on FY2025 [S9, F58-F62]. Two receipts fall inside the valuation window. GEMS paid a US$200.0m FY2026 interim on 22 October 2026, after the 30 June balance sheet, of which DSSA's 51.0% is US$102.0m — carried as a bridge item and leaving the parent's pro-forma net debt lower by that amount [S25, F88, F96]. The subsidiary's own covered model also prices a FY2026 final, payable by the IDX norm on 30 June 2027 and excluded from the ex-final house target, at a forward dividend of Rp805/share, of which DSSA's 51.0% is the second bridge receipt [S20]. The final is not declared, so it is carried below certainty: the subsidiary declared and paid a final of US$500.0m for each of FY2023 and FY2024 [F60, F61] and paid the FY2026 interim in October [F88], which makes a final the established pattern but still a forecast; the shortfall if none is declared is the parent's controlling receipt, and the bridge probability records it [S20]. Both receipts are in the bridge; neither is inside the GEMS mark, so neither is counted twice. The discount is a hoarding discount — cash arrives and is not passed on — not a dead channel.

**The discount.** The house base rate is that a holdco discount persists indefinitely within its band, and a narrower discount needs a dated catalyst that upstreams cash [S0]. There are two buyback precedents. A 2023 buyback took 484 USD m of stock off the market, of which 1,516 million shares, 19.7% of issued capital, still sits in treasury; part was reissued in 2024 for 48.9 USD m [S9]. The second is live: the IDR1.00tn buyback that began on 19 October 2026 and runs to 18 January 2027 [S28]. Both are small against market value — the live programme is about a hundredth of it — and neither is a recurring distribution, so neither passes the card's dated-upstream test. The policy permits up to 30.0% of net profit and the parent has never paid a dividend, saying its subsidiaries need the capital [S9, S0]: that is the card's definition of a holdco that deserves the widest discount in its range. We therefore charge 40%, the wide end of the persistent band.

The peer distribution is measured, not asserted. The house comps put ADRO, BRPT, CUAN and FOLK at thirty per cent, ASII at thirty, TOBA at forty, BNBR at thirty-eight, BHIT at forty and IMJS at sixty, so the median and the mode are both thirty and forty is the wide end, not the middle [S0]. We do not charge the peer median: the hoarding law, not the comps, sets this name's warranted discount, because the parent collects the subsidiary's dividends and passes none on. The non-enforcement structure — the related-party flow, the treasury overhang and the cross-guarantees [S9, F46-F67] — points the same way. The OJK trading sanction is not a second discount: the konglo card assigns it to the lens, and it is counted there once [S10, S14]. Even at the peer median the parts would sit far below the price; the wide-end charge widens the gap in the same direction and does not change the SELL [S0, S9].

The sum of the parts is Rp185 a share; grown at the cost of equity for a year with no dividend leg it is Rp208, and probability-weighted across the business scenarios Rp206 — the fundamental value the konglo lens uses [S0]. The price is Rp625, 3.4x today's value and well above that twelve-month figure; the -29.5% figure is the return to the lens target only [S0].

**The konglo lens.** The engine measures the log premium of 1.2 [S0] and assumes only a share closes in twelve months because the marginal price is set by float: 21.5% of the capital trades [S9, S0]. The closing share is slowed by HSC listing, exit from the IHSG and the index family, and the live sanction [S15, S16, S10, S14]. The exit is now fact rather than a calendar item: 81 HSC names, DSSA and GEMS among them, left the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 and their index weight was redistributed to the remaining constituents [S30]. The lens is run over three regime scenarios, weighted (base at 50%): **bear** closes 85% of the gap for Rp248; **base** closes 45% for Rp405; **bull** closes none and the premium holds for Rp704 [S0]. Probability-weighted, the target is Rp441. The 31 October restitution statement, reported on 5 November, adds no lens flag: it is part of the same enforcement case the lens already counts, and it states no amount, so it changes neither the closing share nor the fundamental [S31]. We do not shade the parts toward or away from the market price [S0].

**What the price implies.** The engine's reverse DCF cannot solve the price inside the discount range: it searches for the holdco discount that would reproduce the Rp625 price from the parts, and the price sits above the undiscounted parts, so no positive discount brackets it [S0]. We disclose the implication directly instead. The parts are worth Rp185 a share after the 40% discount, and even at a zero discount they would be worth only the undiscounted marked value; the price is above that, so the market is paying a premium to the marked parts, not a discount [S0, S20]. The reverse-DCF answer is therefore a negative discount — a premium — and the konglo lens, not the DCF, is what keeps part of it. The same reading applies to the cross-checks: at the current FY2025A multiples of 23.2x earnings and 2.9x book [S0] the quoted price already assumes a re-rating the parts do not support, which is why the own-history P/E and P/BV are dropped rather than blended. Dropping them is the largest single choice in the target, and it is made because they are struck on the tape the regulator found manipulated [S10, S13, S14]; the peer set the house uses for holdcos (ADRO, BRPT, CUAN and FOLK at thirty per cent, ASII at thirty and TOBA, BNBR, BHIT and IMJS wider) supports a discount, not a multiple-of-earnings mark for this name [S0, S9].

**Look-through earnings and leverage.** DSSA's look-through earnings are US$131.7m, the 51.0% share of the coal subsidiary's FY2025A parent profit, against reported parent profit of US$230.5 [S20, S0]. Coal is the largest single contributor but not the whole earnings engine: the non-coal parts supply the balance, a little over two-fifths on the last audited year, and the earlier draft's claim that they contribute little was wrong. Those non-coal earnings sit in segments we mark at book because no segmental operating profit is published; that is the disclosure gap, not a claim that they earn nothing. The subsidiary's own leverage is low — net debt of US$22.3m on equity of US$702.5m [S20] — but the parent's consolidated balance sheet is not: it carries net debt of 910.6, 1.9x EBITDA [S0], because the parent's shelf bonds and sukuk (Phase IV alone Rp0.3tn plus Rp1.2tn) and the non-coal segments' borrowings sit inside the consolidation [S9, F68, F69, F43]. Where the debt sits is the holdco card's test: the coal subsidiary is nearly unlevered, and the leverage is at the parent and in the non-coal parts, whose segment liabilities of 2,121 USD m are already deducted in their net-book marks [S9]. The consolidated leverage is therefore carried inside the parts, not added again at holdco level, and the parent's value is not a levered bet on the coal price [S0, S9]. On the discount itself, the record holds no archived five-year series of price against marked parts (the name has been reclassified and split twice, and no historical SOTP exists), so the 40% is anchored on the house holdco base rate and the peer discounts above, not on a five-year mean we cannot strike [S0]. The current discount to the parts is a premium, at the top of nothing in that record.

The grid is driven by the discount and the cost of equity and reports pre-lens values; it does not bracket the target because the lens adds most of the distance to the price, and it does not bracket the share price because the price requires a negative discount [S0]. The reverse-DCF implication above and the konglo lens are the two legs that reach it. Section five shows the subsidiary's bear target effect instead.

**Currency.** The model translates a USD-reporting group into rupiah at the spot rate, while the house macro deck carries a slightly weaker FY2027E rate [S0]. The difference is about one per cent and moves the target one-for-one; we disclose it rather than blend two FX paths, because the business earns in dollars and the rupiah target is a translation, not a forecast of the exchange rate [S0].

On this method the target is set by the marked parts and the discount; the largest part is the subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental value, imported from its own model. The engine's scenario table can only shock the holdco discount, because a covered holding is marked at its pre-lens fundamental value and cannot be re-priced inside a DSSA scenario, so the table's cases are discount scenarios [S0]. **Bear** (30%): the governance file escalates, the coal marker normalises and the discount widens ten points beyond the wide end of the band to fifty per cent, giving Rp154 today and Rp173 in twelve months [S0]. The conditional asset tail is worse and is stated rather than modelled: at the subsidiary's own published bear target [S20] the controlling stake is worth about a third of its base mark, which alone takes the marked parts down nearly a third, and a ten per cent haircut to the two fallback book marks takes the parent's fundamental down by roughly two-fifths before the lens — that is the arithmetic behind the bear narrative, and it is why the bear weight is 30% rather than lower [S20, S9]. The 30% weight is therefore set against the discount-only bear value in the table, not against the asset tail: if the tail were capitalised in the bear leg the probability-weighted fundamental would be about a tenth below Rp206 and the target below Rp441, in the same direction as the pre-lens mark but from a separate cause. The engine cannot re-price the covered holding inside a DSSA scenario, so the tail is disclosed at full strength rather than forced into a discount shock that would misstate it [S0, S20]. The business and regime sets are combined under the konglo card's independence convention, not because the two are believed independent for this name: a governance escalation or a coal-price fall plausibly drives both. Under that convention the joint-bear weight is the product of 30% and 25%; if the two bear events were perfectly correlated the joint-bear weight would be the smaller of the two, many times the product, and the downside would be the deeper of the two bear values. The convention is disclosed because the card requires it, and the honest reading is that positive correlation makes the joint bear more likely, not rarer [S0, S20]. The mirror is the joint-bull path: the business bull at Rp243 with the regime bull at Rp704, a weight that is the product of 25% and 25% under the same convention. The same positive correlation makes the joint bull likelier too, so the convention treats the upside as conservatively as the downside [S0, S20]. Three structure tails sit outside every mark. First, the cross-guarantee stack: DSSA guarantees EMR facilities of Rp3.6tn, Rp0.4tn and Rp2.0tn and the PT SMPlus data-centre facility of Rp0.4tn [S9, F63-F66]. These are facility plafon, not drawn balances — the accounts do not split drawn from undrawn — so a call on the full stack is about a seventh of the gross parts and would wipe out the capitalised parent overhead many times over; it is sized as a bear tail on the maximum, not netted in the base, and the undrawn share is disclosed as unknown rather than assumed away [S9]. Second, dilution: the annual report's funding waterfall runs internal cash, then short-term debt, then long-term debt, then new shares [S9]; we found no announced rights issue or placement in the sources reviewed, a checked absence rather than proof [S9]. A discounted placement against a controlled price is the classic per-share leak in this structure. Third, the criminal, restitution and refinancing tail: OJK says the parties facing criminal sanctions may be announced within the week [S27]; at the BEI Media Gathering on 31 October, reported on 5 November, it added that it is calculating the funds that could be returned to investors affected by the DSSA, BREN and CUAN cases, while stating no amount, no timing and no payer and saying it could not yet confirm the mechanism or the sum [S31]. The payer is the live question, and the report tests the three routes the evidence allows. The administrative fines were paid by the related parties, not the issuers [S21], and the named recipient was PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the 59.9% controlling shareholder [S26]. If restitution is levied on the same controller, it is a funding call on the shareholder of a 21.5% free-float name; the report checked for a pledge of the controller's DSSA stake and found none disclosed, and no stake sale, margin call or other controller liquidity event is disclosed in the sources reviewed [S9, F74]. If it is charged to the issuer, it is an unquantified liability on DSSA's balance sheet; if to the brokers, it sits outside the group. No route is given a table weight because the source states no amount, timing or payer [S31]. The controller route would not add a second lens flag — the enforcement flag is already counted — but it would widen the warrant for the discount and is the signpost to watch [S10, S14, S31]. Separately the group carries consolidated net debt of 910.6 against FY2025 FCFF of -99.4 and pays no parent dividend [S0, S9]. No source assigns that tail a probability, so it is not given a table weight; the mechanism is a suspension or control change at the controlling shareholder plus a parent refinancing, its value range is the wide end of the discount held for longer, and the konglo lens already slows compression on the enforcement flag. A criminal party list that names an issuer director, or a restitution order naming the issuer as payer, is the signpost that would move the discount to the wide end and keep it there [S13, S27, S31]. **Bull**: a dated capital-allocation signal — the GEMS FY2026 final dividend payable by 30 June 2027 upstreaming to DSSA, the buyback now running through 18 January 2027 completing, a first dividend to DSSA holders or a stake sale — narrows the discount, with the 58Mt plan delivered and technology already doubling [S6, S9, S12, S20, S28]: a value of Rp216 and a target of Rp243, with base at 45% [S0]. The data-centre/technology option is deliberately not carried above book: the D-Hub parcels are marked at the independent appraisal, the KMG-LG Sinarmas data-centre package (Rp1.2tn, F67) is inside the KMG segment's book, the flagship AI-ready data-centre project has no disclosed return, and no segment-return disclosure exists, so a project value would be invented; the bull credits the operating leverage it gives the technology line and the discount, not a project value [S29, F92-F94, S9, F67]. Even at the subsidiary's own bull target the parent's lens target stays below the price: the largest component is a covered subsidiary's mark the parent does not control [S9].

**The subsidiary's own bull face.** The probability-weighted base holds GEMS at its pre-lens fundamental. For scale, the subsidiary's own bull target is Rp12,109/share and its market quote is Rp7,150/share, against the pre-lens fundamental mark of Rp6,094/share and the post-lens house target of Rp6,661/share [S20]. At the bull target the GEMS row rises from the pre-lens mark of Rp6,094/share to Rp12,109/share — an uplift of roughly double the row's marked value, close to one billion US dollars and more than half the base-case fundamental per share — taking the fundamental to roughly half again today's Rp206 and the lens target still below the Rp625; at the market quote of Rp7,150/share the uplift is smaller. We state the marks rather than a recomputed target because the engine marks a covered holding at its pre-lens fundamental and cannot re-price it inside a DSSA scenario; the sensitivity is outside the probability-weighted base [S0, S20].

**The subsidiary's own free-float step.** DSSA's float is compliant, but the largest part's is not. GEMS's free float is 10.1% against the 12.5% first step due 31 March 2027 [F102, F106], inside DSSA's twelve-month window. The subsidiary's model carries the deadline as a regime flag and a new-share remedy of about US$55.1m at a fifty per cent probability; DSSA's 51.0% share is about US$28.1m, roughly one per cent of the parts before the probability [S20]. That dilution sits inside the GEMS mark the SOTP imports, so it is disclosed and not deducted a second time. If the remedy is executed as new shares, the effect on DSSA's value is already in the imported mark; if the controller sells a block instead, the dilution is absent but the free float rises, which is the non-dilutive route the rule allows [S20, S19].

**The konglo regime scenarios.** The lens reads the price at 3.4x fundamental value and asks how much of the 1.2 log gap the regime lets close [S0]. DSSA is on the HSC list and was among the 81 HSC names removed from the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026, a list that includes GEMS, with the removed weight redistributed to the remaining constituents [S15, S16, S30]; it was deleted from the MSCI Global Standard and FTSE Large Cap indexes in 2026 [S17, S18]; and the controlling shareholder carries an OJK sanction whose administrative fines the related parties have now paid, with criminal escalation still open [S10, S13, S14, S21]. DSSA's own free float of 21.5% clears the raised fifteen per cent minimum, so no forced supply step sits in the parent's own window; the subsidiary's step, set out above, is the one that does [S0, S19]. OJK says HSC status alone is not a breach and attracts no sanction, but the more actively traded HSC names face further review and issuers are pressed to refloat, which the exchange presents as the route off the list [S30]. The dated catalysts are the MSCI Standalone consultation, feedback closing on 30 April 2027 with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S22], the IDX free-float deadlines from 31 March 2027 [S24], and the enforcement file [S13].

The MSCI consultation is a binary inside the window, and both branches are carried. The proposal adopted is the regime-bear branch: Indonesia moves to Standalone, the index-increase freeze is not reversed, and the regime weights put a quarter on it. The proposal rejected is the regime-bull branch: the freeze lifts, the HSC names become eligible for index re-inclusion again, and the regime weights put a quarter on it too. The index-flow effect is not a sourced issuer-level number, so it enters through the lens's regime weights rather than as an extra cash-flow item; a rejection is not given a separate value because the lens's bull branch already keeps the full premium (a zero closing share), and that is the most value an index-flow change can carry for this name without inventing a flow estimate [S22, S0]. The bear case is that the premium the lens keeps is what the 2026 regime is dismantling, so a faster unravel is a real risk.

Five risks carry weight. **Governance (high likelihood, high impact)**: the controlling shareholder, PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, has been fined over manipulation of DSSA's shares, the related parties have paid the administrative penalties in full, exchange members were sanctioned, and the regulator now says the parties facing criminal sanctions may be announced within the week and that the administrative track can proceed to criminal prosecution under the una via principle [S14, S10, S13, S21, S26, S27]. On 31 October, reported on 5 November, OJK opened a restitution leg — funds potentially returned to investors in the three cases, with no amount, timing or payer stated and the mechanism unconfirmed [S31]. The restitution leg adds duration and an unquantified liability question to the file rather than a modelled cost; together with the criminal track we read it as a regime factor the konglo lens carries [S0, S31]. **Capital allocation (high likelihood, high impact)**: capex absorbs essentially all of group EBITDA, the parent receives the subsidiary's distributions but has never paid a dividend, and the equity has almost no yield support beyond the small buyback [S0, S9, S28]. The Rp3.1tn D-Hub land purchase is the same pattern in a single transaction: an affiliate sale executed at its independent appraised value, fair on the evidence but a further commitment of parent cash to the data-centre build rather than to holders [S29]. **Coal-market (medium likelihood, medium impact)**: the coal stake is marked at the subsidiary's pre-lens fundamental value, so a lower coal marker lowers the largest part directly [S9, S20]. **Disclosure (high likelihood, medium impact)**: no segmental operating profit is published for the largest book-value segments; a technology-profit disclosure would be the biggest positive change [S9]. **Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact)**: the group reports in dollars, so the rupiah value of the parts moves with the exchange rate while the businesses do not [S0].
A dated action that distributes cash to DSSA's own shareholders — a dividend, buyback or stake sale — would justify a narrower discount [S9], while a criminal escalation widens it [S13, S10].

**The konglo profile.** DSSA is the Sinar Mas group's energy and infrastructure holding, the Widjaja family's listed vehicle and the parent of the separately listed coal miner [S9]. The controlling holding company holds 59.9%; the audited register puts public and treasury shares together at 40.1%, of which treasury is 19.7%, leaving a public float in the low twenties [S9]. The lens uses the datapack's 21.5% IDX registry figure [S0]. The konglo registry's free-float source points at the GEMS interim-dividend article, which contains no float figure; the registry correction stays open with the Director, and until the IDX/KSEI registration is archived this report cites the audited register for the composition and the pack for the lens input [S0, S9, S25]. DSSA's float clears the raised fifteen per cent minimum [S0, S19], but the largest part's does not: GEMS is 10.1% free against the 12.5% first step due 31 March 2027, and the parent's share of the subsidiary's new-share remedy sits inside the GEMS mark used here [S20, F102, F106]. DSSA is on the HSC list and was among the HSC names removed from the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026, a list that includes GEMS [S15, S16, S30], and was deleted from the MSCI Global Standard and FTSE Large Cap indexes in 2026 [S17, S18]. The exchange and OJK are pressing HSC issuers to refloat to cut ownership concentration; that is the stated route off the list and the regime item to watch for this name [S30]. The live enforcement item is the OJK manipulation sanction against PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the controlling shareholder, the largest in the regulator's history: the related parties have paid the administrative fines — IDR2.10tn across the three cases, the DSSA-related share IDR1.50tn — while the criminal file stays open and OJK says the parties facing criminal sanctions may be announced within the week [S10, S13, S14, S21, S26, S27]. At the BEI Media Gathering on 31 October, reported on 5 November, OJK said it is also calculating restitution for investors affected by the three cases, with no amount, timing or payer stated and the mechanism still unconfirmed [S31]. The marginal price is set by the public float — about a fifth of the capital — not by the whole register, and the controller plus treasury hold the rest [S9, S0].

**Structure flags.** Cross-guarantees: DSSA guarantees EMR facilities of Rp3.6tn, Rp0.4tn and Rp2.0tn and the PT SMPlus data-centre facility of Rp0.4tn [S9, F63-F66], contingent claims disclosed and not netted in the parts. These are facility plafon, not drawn balances: the accounts disclose the maximum guaranteed amount and do not split drawn from undrawn, so the bear tail uses the full stack and the report says so rather than presenting it as an outstanding claim [S9]. Treasury: the 2023 buyback left 1,516 million shares, or 19.7% of issued capital, in treasury [S9, F46, F47] — potential supply and a governance overhang; the IDR1.00tn buyback now running from 19 October 2026 to 18 January 2027 is funded from internal cash and will add to that block [S28, S9]. Pledges: the report discloses pledges of GEMS-group shares and receivables for the subsidiary's bank facilities [S9, F74]; we found no disclosure of a pledge of the controlling shareholder's DSSA stake, a checked absence, not proof. Dilution: the stated funding waterfall runs internal cash, then short-term debt, then long-term debt, then new shares [S9]; no rights issue or placement is announced in the sources reviewed, but the channel is live [S9]. Related-party assets: the data-centre build runs through PT LG Sinarmas Technology Solutions at Rp1.2tn [S9, F67], and allocating assets between listed and unlisted vehicles is the family's choice [S9]. Related-party land moves both ways: on 29 October 2026 BSDE unit Surya Inter Wisesa signed a PPJB to sell 16.6 ha in the D-Hub SEZ at BSD City to DSSA unit SMPlus Cakrawala Cipta Gemilang for Rp3.1tn, 5.7% of the group's 30 June equity and just under the independent appraisal of Rp3.12tn; the disclosure calls it an affiliate transaction by family relationship but not a conflict-of-interest transaction, and the appraiser found it fair [S23, S29, F89]. The FY2025 accounts also record the 6 February 2025 related-party purchase of land by KMG, a subsidiary, from BSDE, without a disclosed value in the events calendar [S9]. The priced D-Hub parcel is already inside the group's consolidated equity as cash converted to land; it is not separately valued in the parts because no project return is disclosed. Both are related-party asset moves that widen the warranted discount even where the price is fair.

**Ownership and the sanction.** Minority holders have no practical influence over board composition or the decision to reinvest [S9]. The authority imposed an administrative fine of Rp1.5tn on PT Sinar Mas Tunggal, the controlling shareholder, over manipulation of DSSA's shares, found the manipulation planned and structured and price-lifting, sanctioned 9 exchange members and warned eight sales staff, and handed the letters over on 21 October; the 1 November enforcement list names PT Sinar Mas Tunggal explicitly [S10, S14, S26]. On 30 October it confirmed that the related parties, not the issuers, have paid the fines in full and that the money is in the state treasury: IDR2.10tn across the three cases, the DSSA-related share IDR1.50tn [S21]. It will escalate to a criminal investigation if the evidence supports one, calls the DSSA conduct a criminal market-manipulation act and the sanction the largest in its history, and continues to summon 12 securities-firm directors plus individual and foreign corporate parties; on 1 November the OJK chair said the parties facing criminal sanctions may be announced within the week and framed the track as running from administrative sanctions to criminal prosecution under the una via principle [S13, S21, S27]. At the BEI Media Gathering on 31 October, reported on 5 November, the regulator added a restitution leg: it is calculating the funds that could be returned to investors affected by the three cases, says it cannot yet confirm the mechanism or the amount, and calls the return of funds unusual in its administrative sanctions [S31]. The statement names no payer, and the fines already paid came from the related parties, not the issuers [S21], so no liability is attributed to DSSA here; a mechanism that reaches the issuer's balance sheet is the governance question the development opens, not a base-case cost [S31]. On the house framework this is a manipulation-class flag; the konglo card routes it to the regime lens, so it slows the premium's compression there and is not counted a second time in the holdco discount [S10, S11, S13, S14].

**Dividend and ESG.** The policy permits up to 30.0% of net profit [S9] and the parent has paid none to its own shareholders, on the company's stated explanation that its subsidiaries require the capital [S9]. The subsidiary does pay: the cash flow and its dividend note show distributions to all shareholders, of which the parent receives the controlling share [S9, F58-F61]. An upstream that arrives at the parent and stops there is the whole cost of the structure — a hoarding discount — and it is why the dividend-yield method is dropped and the holdco discount is charged at the wide end of the band rather than at the peer median [S0, S9]. On ESG the exposures are the ordinary ones for Indonesian thermal coal at the subsidiary, plus the governance sanction, on which this name would not pass a controlling-shareholder conduct screen today [S10], and a transition claim resting on disclosure too thin to underwrite [S9, S6].

The regulatory file, the buyback calendar and the index calendar carry the dates. The sanction letters were handed over on 21 October to the sanctioned parties and exchange members [S14, S13]; the 1 November enforcement list named PT Sinar Mas Tunggal [S26]; by 30 October the related parties had paid the administrative fines in full [S21]; and the OJK chair says the criminal-sanction list may follow within the week [S27]. On 31 October, at the BEI Media Gathering in Mandalika, OJK said, reported on 5 November, it is calculating restitution for investors affected by the three cases, with no amount, no timing and no payer stated [S31]; that calculation is an undated watch item because the source gives no deadline. Whether the issuer itself faces action, whether the investigation reaches the courts, and whether the restitution mechanism touches the issuer's balance sheet are what set the governance discount [S10, S11, S21, S31]. The HSC names left the IHSG calculation on 2 November 2026 — 81 of them, DSSA and GEMS included, with the removed weight redistributed to the remaining constituents — and OJK has said the status alone carries no sanction while the active names face review and issuers are pressed to refloat [S16, S30]. The buyback runs to 18 January 2027 [S28], the IDX free-float step lands on 31 March 2027 [S19] — the same date GEMS must lift its float from 10.1% to 12.5% [S20, F106] — and the MSCI Standalone consultation closes on 30 April 2027 with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S22]; both MSCI branches, adoption and rejection, are in section five. The rest are undated watch items [S9]. The HSC exit on 2 November 2026, the buyback end on 18 January 2027 and the GEMS FY2026 final dividend, payable by the IDX norm on 30 June 2027, are the dated items that could move the discount and the upstream respectively [S16, S28, S20].

The monitorables are method-specific. A first dividend or a stake sale at DSSA, or the buyback now running being repeated rather than ending as a one-off, would attack the discount directly; the subsidiary's upstream already reaches the parent, so the missing leg is a durable parent payout [S9, S28]. Segmental operating profit and capital employed for technology, power and chemicals would let us mark those parts on their own cards instead of at fallback book [S9]. And who pays for the data centre and broadband build, at what return, is the item that would most change the parts valuation [S6, S9]. On the regulatory file, a restitution amount or mechanism that names DSSA as payer would turn the governance tail from an unquantified risk into a modelled claim; it is the specific disclosure to watch [S31].

bear.narrative: Built from the bear drivers, not the discount alone. The engine's SOTP marks a covered holding at its pre-lens fundamental value and cannot re-price it inside a scenario, so the table's bear leg widens the holdco discount ten points beyond the wide end of the band to 50% [S9], which is the policy stress a conglomerate can carry in this model. The MSCI proposal is adopted at the 30 June 2027 decision, moving Indonesia to Standalone and removing the index-increase freeze's upside rather than lifting it [S22]. The conditional asset tail is stated after it and is not double-counted in the table: at the subsidiary's own published bear target the parent's 51% mark is about a third of the house mark [S20], which alone takes the marked parts down nearly a third, and a ten per cent haircut to the two fallback book marks (power and technology, the largest non-coal parts) takes the parent's fundamental down by roughly two-fifths before the lens [S9]. The governance file escalates to a criminal investigation and the Rp6.42tn cross-guarantee plafon becomes a live claim inside the same tail [S9, F63-F66]. The bear weight is 30% to carry that conditional tail, but the table's bear leg is a discount-only value: the tail is stated separately and is not double-counted in it, so the 30% weight is set against a severity the table's bear value does not contain, and capitalising the tail would take the probability-weighted fundamental and the target lower than the figures shown. The business and regime sets are combined under the konglo card's independence convention, not because the two are believed independent for this name: a governance escalation or a coal-price fall plausibly drives both, and §5 shows the positively-correlated joint-bear sensitivity.

bull.narrative: Built from the bull drivers. The coal subsidiary delivers its 58Mt plan and holds the GEMS base house mark [S12, S20]; the FY2026 final dividend is paid by 30 June 2027 and the buyback running to 18 January 2027 is repeated, or a first dividend at DSSA itself finally upstreams cash to the parent's holders [S9, F44, S28]. The MSCI Standalone proposal is rejected at the 30 June 2027 decision and the index-increase freeze is lifted, re-opening the HSC names to passive flows [S22]. Technology revenue, already roughly doubled in the first half, earns its book and the discount narrows to the peer median at 30% [S6, F20, S9]. The data-centre/technology option is deliberately not credited above book: the D-Hub parcels are carried at the independent appraisal (the purchase price sits just below it), the flagship AI-ready data-centre project has no disclosed return, and no segment-return disclosure exists, so any uplift would be invented; the bull leg is the discount, the upstream and the index-relief branch, not a project value [S29, F92-F94, S9]. Even here the parts do not reach the market's price.
